title: Rahaf: A Life Recast by War
summary: My name is Rahaf. I am a mother of seven, and I am from Gaza. My family of nine lives in a tent, in circumstances that are very hard.
content:
Themes: motherhood · displacement · daily survival · children's hopes

My name is Rahaf. I am a mother of seven, and I am from Gaza. My family of nine lives in a tent, in circumstances that are very hard.

Most of my days go to keeping my children alive. I light fires and spend hours cooking food and heating water for them. Even wood costs us something we can barely spare, but there is no other way.

The tent is not a safe place. It is full of insects, fleas, cockroaches and rats. At night I am afraid for my children, and I can’t always protect them from what crawls around them.

Still, my children keep dreaming. One day I asked them to draw what they wished for. They drew a home, safety, security, peace and freedom, the things the war took from them. When I look at those drawings, I see how much they have lost, and how much they still hope for.

My youngest son is not yet three. He was born during the war, so he has never known anything else. Recently he finally got a toy, and I watched his face light up. It was the first real joy I had seen in him in a long time. I wish a child’s happiness didn’t have to be so rare.

Another of my sons is quiet and patient far beyond his years. There is a story behind his smile that he doesn’t tell. He doesn’t ask for much, only a chance to live in peace.

So I ask people to stand with us and not to leave my children alone. They are suffering in these tents, and we need help.

But I also want you to know that we are still here, still hoping. For their sake, we endure and dream of a brighter day. Our dreams are small, but they are worth living for.

title: Aya: A Life Recast by War
summary: My name is Aya. I’m 21 years old, and I’m from Gaza. I’m a journalism student who has always dreamed of telling stories, including my own.
content:
Themes: education · photography · family responsibility · young ambition

My name is Aya. I’m 21 years old, and I’m from Gaza. I’m a journalism student who has always dreamed of telling stories, including my own.

The war has made everything harder. I dream of completing my bachelor’s degree, and I have never stopped trying, even when continuing my education has felt almost impossible.

Alongside my studies, I help support my family. I carry this responsibility with me every day, often feeling as though I’m fighting for both my future and theirs.

My health has also become part of my journey, adding another challenge to an already difficult reality.

I picked up a camera because I wanted to do something with my hands and my eyes rather than simply wait. Photography gave me a way to express myself, document the world around me, and pursue a future I could build for myself and my family. I dream of turning this passion into a career and a source of income.

Through my lens, I show what life in Gaza looks like: ruined buildings, streets scarred by strikes, a pot resting over a fire, and smoke rising into the sky. I don’t blur these realities or look away from them. I choose to protect my own face, but I want the world to see the place where I live and the reality its people face every day.

I’m sharing my story because I want people to see beyond the headlines about Gaza. Behind the news are young people with dreams, unfinished degrees, families to support, and talents they are determined to develop. I am one of them, still trying to build a future despite everything that stands in my way.

title: Duha: A Life Recast by War
summary: My name is Duha, and I am a mother from Gaza. My daughter’s name is Wateen Al-Rouh.
content:
Themes: motherhood · bereavement · childbirth during war · a child's future

My name is Duha, and I am a mother from Gaza. My daughter’s name is Wateen Al-Rouh.

I had always dreamed of building a family. But before I could begin that life, I lost my husband while I was still pregnant with our daughter. I was six months pregnant, and the grief took a heavy toll on me. My health was fragile, and my condition was unstable.

Wateen was born on July 26, 2025, by Caesarean section, in the middle of the war. She weighed 2.9 kilograms. I gave birth in a hospital in southern Gaza as explosions sounded nearby and fear filled the air. I held my newborn daughter, knowing that her father would never have the chance to meet her.

Just one day after giving birth, I had to leave the hospital because it was no longer safe. I carried my newborn back to a tent. She was only one day old. Since then, our suffering has continued to grow. The heat is unbearable, insects are everywhere, smoke from open fires fills the air, and hunger is a constant presence in our lives.

Providing even the most basic necessities for my daughter, including milk and diapers, is a daily struggle. Wateen entered this world having already lost her father before she was born. From the very beginning of her life, she has been surrounded by hardships no child should have to face.

I am sharing our story because I want my daughter to have the chance to grow up in safety, with the opportunity to live a life beyond survival. I want her future to hold the possibilities that every child deserves: security, care, and the freedom to dream.

Every act of kindness, no matter how small, can make a meaningful difference in the lives of my daughter and me. More than anything, I want Wateen to have the chance to grow up in a world where she can experience the safety and happiness that every child deserves.

title: Waseem: A Life Recast by War
summary: My name is Waseem, and I’m from Gaza. I’m sharing my story to raise awareness about what my family and I have endured, and to hold on to hope for a better future.
content:
Themes: home · loss · family · hope amid destruction

My name is Waseem, and I’m from Gaza. I’m sharing my story to raise awareness about what my family and I have endured, and to hold on to hope for a better future.

My family’s home is gone. It was the place where we felt safe, where our lives unfolded, and where we kept the things that mattered to us. Today, it lies in ruins. Standing where our home once stood reminds me of how much we have lost: our sense of security, our belongings, and the life we once knew. Since then, every day has been a struggle.

Yet, I keep reminding myself that the war has taken so much from us, but it has not extinguished the roots of hope in my heart. They are still alive, even among the rubble.

As we try to rebuild our lives, I am raising donations to help my family endure these difficult circumstances. We urgently need basic necessities, and every contribution brings us a little closer to meeting those needs and facing the days ahead.

Even in the midst of so much hardship, the children around me remind me why we must keep going. Their strength amazes me, and seeing a child smile can bring hope back into my day. Life remains uncertain, and each day brings new challenges, but we continue to hold on to one another and find reasons to keep moving forward.

I want people to see what has happened to my home and my city, but also to remember the people who live here. We are more than the destruction surrounding us. We are people with memories, families, dreams, and plans for the future. Despite everything we have lost, we still hope to rebuild our lives and find a measure of stability again.

Every act of support, no matter how small, can make a real difference to my family. Your kindness can help us meet our immediate needs and hold on to the hope that, one day, we will be able to build a safer and more secure future.

Regarding who I am, my name is Waseem and I am from Gaza. I share my story so that people can understand what life here has become, and so that hope is not lost.

As for my home, it was where my family felt safe, and it is now rubble. Standing in the place where our house used to be, I understand how much was taken from us: our safety, and nearly everything we owned. Life has been incredibly hard since then.

When it comes to daily life, every day brings new challenges. My family urgently needs the basic necessities that most people take for granted, and we are trying to rebuild our lives from the ruins.

Regarding the children around me, their strength is one of the things that carries me through the hardest days. One of them still smiles despite everything, and that smile brings hope back into my days. We hold on to life despite the hardships.

When it comes to hope, I try to be honest about what the war has done. It has taken a great deal, but the roots of hope in my heart are still alive. That is not an easy thing to say, but it is what keeps me going.

As for how I want Gaza to be seen, I want people to look at what happened to my home and my city. I also want them to recognize that the people living through it still have hopes and plans, and that we are more than the destruction around us.

title: Marwa: A Life Recast by War
summary: Marwa, from Gaza
content:
Themes: repeated displacement · motherhood · dignity · memory of home

Marwa, from Gaza

My name is Marwa. I am a mother of four, and I am from Gaza.

I used to be a woman with a home, and I didn’t think about what that meant. A home is where the day begins and ends. It’s where my children’s voices fill the rooms and where I know which corner is whose. I never thought of it as something that could be taken, until it was.

Since then, we have moved more than thirteen times. I stopped counting the places a long time ago and started counting what we carried instead, which was less each time. Every move cost us something: a blanket, a photograph, a little more of the life we knew. In the end we lost everything we owned.

What I miss most is not an object. It’s safety, the simple feeling of closing my eyes and trusting that the night will pass quietly. I miss food that arrives without a struggle. I miss dignity, being able to care for my children the way a mother should.

My children are growing up in a world that asks too much of them. Children should dream of toys. Mine dream of food and of a safe place to sleep. When I hear them say it, I have to hold something steady inside myself so they don’t see how heavy it is.

But we are still here. Every morning I wake my children and we begin again. I tell them what mothers have always told their children: that we are together, and that together we are stronger than what surrounds us.

I’m sharing this because I don’t want to be only a name or a number. I’m Marwa, a mother and a woman who loved her home. I’m trying to keep my children safe, fed, and hopeful, and I would like the world to know that we are people, and that we are still here.

title: Diaa: A Life Recast by War
summary: Diaa, from Gaza**
content:
Themes: displacement · hunger · injury · responsibility for family

Diaa, from Gaza**

My name is Diaa. I am a Palestinian from Gaza, and these days I am displaced, living in a tent with my family. There are nine of us.

Before all this, I had a home, and I never gave a thought to what that word held. Now my life is measured in smaller things: whether there is bread today, whether there is water, whether the tent will hold through the night.

Hunger is the hardest part to describe, because it is not only in the stomach. It is in the ears, in the sound of my little sister crying. Her name is Soso. When a child cries from hunger and you have nothing to give her, something in you goes quiet and heavy at the same time. I carry that sound with me all day.

Living this way brings its own weight: the fear that does not leave, and the humiliation of a life stripped down to survival. A man is supposed to be able to provide for the people he loves. Every morning I wake up and try again, and some days I have little to show for it. Still, I try.

My health has not been spared either. I live with the aftermath of an injury, and I have faced fear for my eyesight, a worry that sits beside all the others. Even so, my thoughts keep returning to my family, to the nine of us under one roof of canvas.

I am telling you this because I do not want to disappear into a headline. I am a brother, a son, a man with a family who is still here. We have lost a great deal, but not our names, our love for each other, or our hope that someone, somewhere, is listening.

Part II — Djerba: Jewish Identity, Education, and Belonging

title: Between Three Worlds: Growing Up Jewish in Djerba
summary: I was born in Djerba, where I grew up surrounded by a way of life that was deeply connected to Islamic, Arabic, and Jewish culture. These different influences shaped the environment in which I spent my childhood. Although French culture had become an…
content:
Themes: identity · education · religion · language · belonging

I was born in Djerba, where I grew up surrounded by a way of life that was deeply connected to Islamic, Arabic, and Jewish culture. These different influences shaped the environment in which I spent my childhood. Although French culture had become an important part of Tunisia's history, I personally did not experience much of it growing up. Perhaps my grandparents had known that world more closely, but my own childhood was shaped by a different cultural reality.

Being Jewish in Djerba meant growing up within a society where different religious and cultural traditions existed alongside one another. My experiences were largely defined by this environment, and it was here that I began developing my understanding of my own identity and the world around me.

Looking back, I recognize how much the cultural environment of Djerba influenced my upbringing. It was the world I knew, the traditions I grew up with, and the foundation upon which I built my understanding of what it meant to be Jewish and Tunisian.

title: Three Years Lost: When Shabbat Came Before an Examination
summary: I attended a public school in Djerba as a Jewish student, and throughout my education, I performed exceptionally well. I passed every class, and I was regularly ranked first in my classroom. My teachers knew my academic abilities and were confident that I…
content:
Themes: identity · education · religion · language · belonging

I attended a public school in Djerba as a Jewish student, and throughout my education, I performed exceptionally well. I passed every class, and I was regularly ranked first in my classroom. My teachers knew my academic abilities and were confident that I would successfully continue my education.

Everything changed when I reached sixth grade. At that stage, students had to complete a national examination to qualify officially for high school. I had worked hard for years, and everyone expected me to pass. However, the examination presented a problem that had nothing to do with my academic abilities.

The examinations were scheduled across Friday and the following day. As a Jewish person who observed Shabbat very seriously, I could not simply disregard my religious obligations to sit an examination. I completed the Friday examination, but I could not attend the following one. Consequently, I failed to complete the examination requirements and was unable to progress.

I had to wait another year and attempt the examination again. Yet, when the following year arrived, the same situation repeated itself. Once again, the examination coincided with Shabbat, leaving me in exactly the same position.

After the second attempt, I heard that the president was going to visit Djerba. I gathered several of my friends, and we went hoping that we might get an opportunity to approach him and explain our situation. We managed to see him, but the police and security personnel prevented us from getting close enough to speak with him. Other people seemed to have opportunities to approach him, but we were unable to do so.

Another year passed. By the third attempt, the same examination conflict occurred again. This was the final opportunity I was permitted. After failing to complete the examination for the third time, I was no longer allowed to continue my education.

What makes this experience particularly painful is that I had never struggled academically. I had consistently been among the best students in my school. My inability to progress was not the result of a lack of effort or intellectual ability, but of a conflict between the requirements of the examination system and my religious convictions.

Even today, it hurts to think about the education I never got to complete. I often wonder how different my future might have been if I had been given the opportunity to attend high school and graduate. Nevertheless, I believe that everything happens according to God's plan, and I have learned to accept what was written for me.

title: A President's Visit: The Attempt to Have Our Voices Heard
summary: After my examination difficulties had continued for another year, I began looking for ways to bring attention to our situation. I knew that the president was going to visit Djerba, and I saw this as a possible opportunity to explain what had happened and…
content:
Themes: identity · education · religion · language · belonging

After my examination difficulties had continued for another year, I began looking for ways to bring attention to our situation. I knew that the president was going to visit Djerba, and I saw this as a possible opportunity to explain what had happened and perhaps find someone who could help.

I gathered several of my friends, and together we went hoping to see him. We wanted to approach him, speak with him, and explain our circumstances. It was an opportunity that seemed important, especially because my situation had already cost me an entire year of education.

We did manage to see the president, but getting close enough to speak to him proved impossible. The police and security personnel prevented us from approaching him, and we were left watching from a distance. While other people appeared to have opportunities to interact with him, we could not get near enough to explain why we had come.

We returned without having achieved anything.

For me, that moment represented another missed opportunity. I had already spent years trying to overcome an obstacle that had nothing to do with my academic performance. I was not asking for special treatment because I was a good student; I simply wanted an opportunity to continue my education without having to abandon my religious obligations.

The visit did not change my circumstances. Another year passed, and I eventually reached the final examination attempt I was allowed.

title: The Quran in the Classroom: A Principal Who Defended My Right to Refuse
summary: One experience from my school years that has remained particularly vivid in my memory concerns a teacher who taught Islamic education.
content:
Themes: identity · education · religion · language · belonging

One experience from my school years that has remained particularly vivid in my memory concerns a teacher who taught Islamic education.

During our lessons, this teacher would repeatedly single me out from among the other students and ask me to read passages from the Quran aloud. As a Jewish student, I felt uncomfortable being placed in that position. It was not that I lacked respect for Islam or for the Quran. Rather, I felt that I should not be compelled to participate in something that did not belong to my own religious practice.

On one occasion, the teacher asked me to read. I politely explained that I could not.

She insisted that I had to do it.

I responded, "No, sorry, Miss. I respect you a lot, but I cannot do it."

The disagreement escalated, and she called the principal.

Fortunately, the principal understood my position. His name was Mr. Hamudi, and to this day, I remember him as one of the kindest people I encountered during my school years. He was an exceptionally gentle and compassionate person.

When he intervened, he took my side. He explained to the teacher that I was not obligated to read the Quran and that my religious identity and personal convictions had to be respected.

That moment meant a great deal to me. I had been placed in an uncomfortable situation, but someone in a position of authority recognized that respecting another person's religion also means respecting their right not to participate in another religion's practices.

I have never forgotten Mr. Hamudi. In an environment where I sometimes felt misunderstood, he demonstrated that kindness, understanding, and respect could transcend religious differences.

His intervention remains one of the memories I cherish most from my school years.

title: The Lesson I Never Forgot: Friendship, Courage, and Humiliation in an Arabic Classroom
summary: I remember one particular Arabic lesson that has stayed with me throughout my life.
content:
Themes: identity · education · religion · language · belonging

I remember one particular Arabic lesson that has stayed with me throughout my life.

I was sitting in class with one of my Muslim friends, and we had been given an Arabic assignment. I was particularly good at Arabic, and I was confident in my abilities. After completing the exercise, I believed that my answers were correct.

When the teacher decided to correct the assignment, he randomly selected a student to go to the board and write down the answers. The student completed the exercise, and the teacher announced that his work was correct.

I immediately noticed something was wrong. The answers on the board were not the same as mine, and I was convinced that my own solution was correct. I was so confident that I looked over at my friend's work and told him that he had made a mistake. I explained how I believed the exercise should be solved, and he listened to me and corrected his answers.

That was when the teacher announced that anyone whose work did not follow the exact same method as the student at the board would be punished with a wooden stick.

He began going around the classroom, checking everyone's notebooks.

My friend was examined before me. When the teacher looked through his notebook, my friend realized that he had changed his original answers because of my advice. He turned to me and said something along the lines of, "Come on! I had it right before. Why did you make me change it? Now I'm going to get hit because of you!"

I told him not to worry.

"It's okay, my friend. I'll take responsibility. I'll tell him the truth."

My friend approached the teacher with his notebook, and the teacher was preparing to punish him. Before he could do so, I intervened and explained that I had been the one who told my friend to change his answers. I also insisted that the work written on the board was incorrect and that I was confident in my own solution.

The teacher challenged me. He decided to give me another example involving a similar grammatical construction in Arabic. It is difficult to reproduce the exact exercise in English because the grammatical structures do not translate directly.

The example involved transforming a phrase that essentially meant "the boy was as dumb as a donkey" into another grammatical format.

The teacher directed this question at me in front of the entire classroom. Rather than simply discussing the grammatical principle, he used the opportunity to embarrass me, and the other students laughed.

That moment stayed with me.

I had originally spoken up because I believed I was correct, and I had intervened because I did not want my friend to be punished for following my advice. Instead, I found myself being publicly humiliated.

There is another dimension to this memory that makes it particularly difficult for me to discuss. In my religion, teachers hold an extremely important and almost sacred position. I was raised to value them, respect them, and recognize the responsibility they carry in educating their students.

Even today, it is difficult for me to speak negatively about a teacher. I find it painful to say that an educator behaved wrongly because I have such a deep appreciation for the teaching profession.

But this experience left an impression on me that I have never been able to erase.

title: From Arabic to Hebrew: Discovering a Connection Through Language and Faith
summary: After my time in public school came to an end, I decided to attend a Jewish religious school. It was not a general educational institution where students studied the usual academic subjects. Its primary purpose was to teach Jewish religious traditions, the…
content:
Themes: identity · education · religion · language · belonging

After my time in public school came to an end, I decided to attend a Jewish religious school. It was not a general educational institution where students studied the usual academic subjects. Its primary purpose was to teach Jewish religious traditions, the Torah, and other aspects of Jewish learning.

Interestingly, I found the experience much easier than I had initially expected.

I quickly noticed similarities between Arabic and Hebrew. The two languages shared grammatical structures, linguistic rules, and other elements that made the transition from one to the other surprisingly natural for me.

Because I already had a strong foundation in Arabic, learning Hebrew became considerably easier. I could recognize familiar patterns and understand certain grammatical concepts without having to approach everything from the beginning.

I progressed very quickly and found myself performing exceptionally well compared with my peers.

It was an unexpected discovery. Although I had lost the opportunity to continue my general education, I found another educational environment in which I could develop my knowledge and deepen my connection to my religious heritage.

Learning Hebrew also allowed me to appreciate the linguistic relationship between two languages that had been part of the wider cultural environment of my upbringing.

What initially seemed like a completely new subject became something familiar. My knowledge of Arabic had unexpectedly become a bridge to understanding Hebrew, and that made the experience particularly rewarding.

Part III — The Tunisian Medina: A Craft Passed Between Generations

title: A Profession Learned Beside My Father
summary: I have been working in this profession for as long as I can remember. In many ways, I did not choose this path; I grew up surrounded by it. My father was a craftsman, and from a very young age, I would accompany him to work in the medina. While other children…
content:
Themes: craftsmanship · father and son · work · cultural inheritance

I have been working in this profession for as long as I can remember. In many ways, I did not choose this path; I grew up surrounded by it. My father was a craftsman, and from a very young age, I would accompany him to work in the medina. While other children might spend their days playing or staying at home, I was accustomed to being beside my father, watching him work, helping him with whatever I could, and observing the different stages of his craft. He never needed to sit me down and formally explain everything. I learned by watching, listening, and gradually becoming involved in the work myself. Little by little, what had initially been a way of spending time with my father became a profession that would eventually define much of my life.

This is how many traditional professions were passed down in Tunisia. A father would teach his son, who would eventually teach his own children. Knowledge was not always written down or formally documented; it was carried through experience, through the movement of one's hands, and through years of working alongside someone who had mastered the craft before you. You learned the materials, understood their qualities, recognized what worked and what did not, and developed a sense of precision that could only come with time. It was a way of preserving something without necessarily realizing that you were preserving it.

title: The Balgha and the Work That Once Sustained Us
summary: In the past, traditional shoemaking was an important source of livelihood. People worked because they needed to provide for themselves and their families, and there was a practical purpose behind almost everything they produced. Traditional footwear,…
content:
Themes: craftsmanship · father and son · work · cultural inheritance

In the past, traditional shoemaking was an important source of livelihood. People worked because they needed to provide for themselves and their families, and there was a practical purpose behind almost everything they produced. Traditional footwear, particularly the *balgha*, was part of everyday Tunisian life. People wore these shoes because they were familiar, useful, and suited to the way people lived. At the time, craftsmanship was understood differently. People recognized that making something by hand required effort, patience, and experience. It was not simply a matter of producing an object and selling it; it was about knowing your profession and being able to make something properly.

title: Making Three or Four Pairs While Factories Make Hundreds
summary: Today, however, the situation has changed considerably. The profession has become more difficult, particularly because of the competition from industrial production and the increasing availability of cheaper alternatives. There are people who can produce…
content:
Themes: craftsmanship · father and son · work · cultural inheritance

Today, however, the situation has changed considerably. The profession has become more difficult, particularly because of the competition from industrial production and the increasing availability of cheaper alternatives. There are people who can produce dozens, sometimes even hundreds, of shoes in the time that a traditional craftsman might need to make only a few. I may spend an entire day working carefully on three or four pairs, making sure that every detail is right, while someone else can manufacture a much greater quantity in the same amount of time. But there is a difference between producing something quickly and producing something with care. Quality requires time. It requires attention, experience, and a willingness to concentrate on even the smallest details.

This is one of the greatest challenges facing traditional artisans today. We are competing in a market where quantity and price have become increasingly important, while the time and skill invested in handmade products are not always appreciated. A customer may see two pairs of shoes that look similar and naturally choose the cheaper one without understanding the difference in the materials, the construction, or the work behind each product. Sometimes, people do not realize how much time goes into making something properly. They see the finished shoe, but they do not see the hours of work that preceded it.

title: Changing Materials Without Losing the Craft
summary: The materials themselves have also changed over the years. Traditionally, we worked primarily with leather, using different types depending on the product and the purpose. We used goat leather, sheep leather, and other varieties that were available to us.…
content:
Themes: craftsmanship · father and son · work · cultural inheritance

The materials themselves have also changed over the years. Traditionally, we worked primarily with leather, using different types depending on the product and the purpose. We used goat leather, sheep leather, and other varieties that were available to us. These materials were familiar to craftsmen, and we understood how to work with each one. Today, however, things are different. New materials have entered the market, and customers have developed different preferences. We have had to experiment, introduce new fabrics, explore different combinations, and modify certain aspects of our products. We cannot simply continue working exactly as people did decades ago and expect the market to remain the same.

At the same time, adapting does not mean abandoning everything that came before us. There is a difference between allowing a profession to evolve and losing the qualities that make it distinctive. I believe we can introduce new designs, different colours, and improved materials while still maintaining the identity of traditional Tunisian footwear. We can develop our work without erasing its origins. For example, the *balgha* does not have to remain limited to one particular design or appearance. We can experiment with its colours, improve its construction, and make it attractive to people who might not traditionally wear it. I would like to see more Tunisians, especially younger generations, appreciate these products and incorporate them into their everyday lives.

title: The Old Olive-Wood Table in the Workshop
summary: There is also an important question of quality. When you work with your hands, you develop an understanding of what makes a product durable, comfortable, and well made. You learn to recognize the difference between materials, and you understand that even…
content:
Themes: craftsmanship · father and son · work · cultural inheritance

There is also an important question of quality. When you work with your hands, you develop an understanding of what makes a product durable, comfortable, and well made. You learn to recognize the difference between materials, and you understand that even small changes can affect the final result. A shoe is not simply something that covers the foot. It has to be constructed properly, it has to be comfortable, and it has to withstand everyday use. These are things that cannot always be achieved by rushing through production.

I have seen how the market has evolved, and I understand that people have different expectations today. Everyone wants something accessible, affordable, and readily available. I do not necessarily blame customers for that. People have their own circumstances, and everyone has to consider what they can afford. But I also believe that we should not forget the value of handmade products. There is a reason traditional crafts have survived for so many generations. They represent knowledge and experience that cannot simply be replaced overnight.

title: Keeping a Traditional Profession Alive
summary: Sometimes, when I look around my workshop, I am reminded of how much history can exist within a single place. There are objects here that have been around for generations. I have a table made from olive wood that is approximately 120 or 130 years old. Think…
content:
Themes: craftsmanship · father and son · work · cultural inheritance

Sometimes, when I look around my workshop, I am reminded of how much history can exist within a single place. There are objects here that have been around for generations. I have a table made from olive wood that is approximately 120 or 130 years old. Think about that for a moment: this table existed long before I began working, and it has remained here through so many years of change. It has witnessed different people, different generations, and different periods of life in the medina. Objects like these remind us that our work is connected to something much larger than ourselves.

I do not see my profession as simply a means of earning money. Of course, making a living is essential. This is my source of income, and like everyone else, I have responsibilities. But there is also something meaningful about continuing a profession that was taught to me by my father. When I work, I am not starting from nothing. I am continuing something that existed before me, something that was built through the effort of people whose names and stories may never be recorded anywhere.

I believe that traditional Tunisian craftsmanship deserves more recognition. We have so many products, techniques, and traditions that are part of our cultural identity, yet we do not always give them the attention they deserve. Sometimes, people admire traditional objects when they encounter them abroad, or when they see them presented as part of another country's heritage, but they overlook their importance at home. We should be proud of what we have inherited. Our traditions are not obstacles to progress; they are part of what gives our society its character.

I would like to see traditional craftsmanship develop rather than disappear. I want people to understand that these professions can still have a place in modern Tunisia. We can introduce new ideas, improve the way we work, and make our products more accessible without sacrificing the knowledge and techniques that have been passed down to us. There is no reason why a traditional Tunisian shoe cannot appeal to someone young, someone living abroad, or someone who has never even visited the medina. What matters is that we continue giving these traditions a place in people's lives.

Ultimately, I am doing what I learned from my father. I continue working with the materials, techniques, and knowledge that were introduced to me when I was a child. The world around us may change, customers may change, and the market may become more difficult, but I believe there is still value in making something with your own hands. Every pair of shoes represents time, effort, and a certain understanding of the craft. And as long as there are people willing to learn, work, and appreciate what we produce, there is still a future for this profession.

For me, preserving this craft does not mean refusing to move forward. It means remembering where we came from while finding ways to continue. My father taught me this profession, and I have carried it with me throughout my life. I hope that the knowledge does not end with my generation. Because when a traditional profession disappears, we do not simply lose a way of earning a living. We risk losing a part of our history, our identity, and the stories of the people who built it with their hands.

Source note: Adapted only by dividing the existing shoemaker testimony at distinct thematic transitions.

Part IV — The Jewish Community of La Goulette and Tunis

title: A Synagogue That Is More Than a Place of Prayer
summary: In the interviews and research notes about the Jewish community in La Goulette and Tunis, the synagogue appears as more than a building used for religious services. It is also a place where people encounter one another, exchange news, and remain connected to…
content:
Themes: community · continuity · religious life · family · coexistence

In the interviews and research notes about the Jewish community in La Goulette and Tunis, the synagogue appears as more than a building used for religious services. It is also a place where people encounter one another, exchange news, and remain connected to a community whose numbers have become very small. The notes describe it as a place where individuals can feel part of something larger than their own households. That social function matters especially when fewer families remain and ordinary opportunities to meet have become less frequent.

The material also identifies a practical challenge: communal prayer can depend on a minyan, a quorum of ten people. When the local community is only just large enough to gather that number, each person's participation becomes important. The synagogue therefore represents both continuity and vulnerability. It keeps religious life visible and provides a shared meeting point, but its ability to fulfil that role depends on the continued presence of community members.

The story is not simply that a synagogue survives. It is that a small community continues to use a shared institution to sustain relationships, religious practice, and a sense of belonging.

Source note: Based on interview-analysis notes concerning Daniel Cohen, Massimo, Albert Chiche, Samuel, and Participant A. This is a narrative synthesis, not a verbatim participant transcript.

relatedNarratives.title: The Synagogue as a Place to Pray and to Belong
relatedNarratives.content:
Source: Albert

Albert describes the synagogue as a place with several roles. It is where people gather for prayer, especially on Shabbat and religious holidays, but it is also a place where members of the community meet and speak with one another. After prayers, people may remain to discuss their families, children, daily concerns, and plans for the future.

The synagogue therefore connects religious observance with social continuity. Its importance is not limited to the formal service. It provides a setting in which people can reconnect, exchange news, and maintain relationships within a community that has become much smaller.

Albert mentions the major holidays observed throughout the year, including Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkot, Passover, Shavuot, Purim, and Hanukkah. These occasions bring people together at different points in the calendar and give communal life a recurring structure.

He also explains that synagogues differ in size according to the communities they serve. Some can accommodate more than one hundred people, while smaller ones may gather only fifteen or twenty. This variation reflects the different sizes and circumstances of Jewish communities across Tunisia.

In Albert's account, the synagogue is both a religious institution and a social anchor. It allows traditions to be practiced collectively and gives people a place where they can recognize one another as members of a continuing community. When the population declines, that shared space becomes even more significant.

title: Ten People, One Minyan
summary: The interview material describes a community whose remaining members must think practically about the number of people needed for communal prayer. A minyan requires ten participants. In a much larger community, reaching that number may be routine; in a…
content:
Themes: community · continuity · religious life · family · coexistence

The interview material describes a community whose remaining members must think practically about the number of people needed for communal prayer. A minyan requires ten participants. In a much larger community, reaching that number may be routine; in a community of just over ten people, it can become a central concern.

Albert Chiche's account, as summarized in the research notes, emphasizes how demographic decline changes the practical conditions of religious life. Some synagogues are small, accommodating only around fifteen or twenty people. When the community itself is only slightly larger than the quorum required for certain prayers, the participation of each individual carries unusual weight.

This is one of the clearest ways population decline becomes part of everyday experience. It is not only a matter of historical numbers or the disappearance of institutions. It affects whether a service can take place with the people required, and whether the remaining members can maintain a regular communal rhythm. The story of the minyan is therefore a story about how continuity depends on people showing up for one another.

Source note: Based on interview-analysis notes concerning Daniel Cohen, Massimo, Albert Chiche, Samuel, and Participant A. This is a narrative synthesis, not a verbatim participant transcript.

relatedNarratives.title: Ten People and the Fragility of a Minyan
relatedNarratives.content:
Source: Albert

Albert explains that certain Jewish prayers require a minyan, a quorum of ten people. Without the required number, the service cannot proceed in the usual way. His explanation is brief, but it points to a practical consequence of demographic decline: when a community becomes very small, the presence of each individual can matter greatly.

A minyan is not simply a number on a page. It depends on people being available at the same time and willing or able to attend. In a larger community, gathering ten people may be relatively straightforward. In a much smaller one, arranging the quorum can become a challenge.

Albert's remarks place religious continuity within the realities of community size. The decline in population affects more than the number of families or the visibility of Jewish life in public. It can affect whether a particular prayer service can be held.

This is one reason the remaining relationships and institutions matter. A community needs people who continue to attend, participate, and help sustain its religious life. The importance of each member becomes more visible when there are fewer members overall.

Albert does not describe every logistical difficulty involved in arranging a minyan, so the account should not be expanded into specific scenes that he did not provide. What his answer does establish is the principle: the quorum is required, and the reduced size of the community makes the participation of its members especially consequential.

title: The Neighbour Who Turns on the Light
summary: Albert Chiche's testimony includes a concrete example of cooperation between Jewish residents and their Muslim neighbours. The research notes explain that observant Jewish residents may refrain from operating electrical switches during Shabbat. In some…
content:
Themes: community · continuity · religious life · family · coexistence

Albert Chiche's testimony includes a concrete example of cooperation between Jewish residents and their Muslim neighbours. The research notes explain that observant Jewish residents may refrain from operating electrical switches during Shabbat. In some circumstances, they have relied on a neighbour to turn a light on or off.

The significance of this example lies in its ordinariness. It is not described as a formal agreement or a public declaration about coexistence. It is a small act of practical assistance between people who know one another. The neighbour does not need to share the same religious practice in order to understand that it matters to the person next door.

The example shows how differences can be accommodated through everyday relationships. Religious observance remains important, while neighbourly cooperation makes it easier for people to maintain their practices. The story also reveals a limit: such assistance can support an individual's observance, but it cannot replace the Jewish community members needed for a minyan or for other internal communal activities.

Source note: Based on interview-analysis notes concerning Daniel Cohen, Massimo, Albert Chiche, Samuel, and Participant A. This is a narrative synthesis, not a verbatim participant transcript.

relatedNarratives.title: The Neighbour Who Helped on Shabbat
relatedNarratives.content:
Source: Albert

Albert offers a concrete example of cooperation between Jewish and Muslim neighbours: assistance during Shabbat. He explains that observant Jews traditionally refrain from certain activities from Friday evening until Saturday evening. In the examples he gives, a Jewish resident might ask a Muslim neighbour to switch on a light at a particular time or to turn something off later.

The significance of the example lies in its ordinariness. It is not presented as a formal agreement or an exceptional public gesture. It is a practical arrangement between people who know one another and are accustomed to helping when a neighbour needs something. The request is understood within the rhythm of everyday life.

Albert says that Jews and Muslims could live in the same Hara in Djerba. When a Jewish person needed assistance, a Muslim neighbour could help. The Shabbat example makes that broader statement tangible: coexistence is visible in a small act carried out at a specific moment in the week.

The account also reveals how religious difference can be accommodated without requiring people to abandon their own practices. The Jewish neighbour observes Shabbat; the Muslim neighbour offers assistance. Each understands the other's routine well enough for the arrangement to work.

Albert's memory presents mutual support as something practical rather than abstract. It is expressed through attention, familiarity, and willingness to help. In this instance, a light being switched on or off becomes a small but meaningful example of how neighbours can make room for one another's religious lives.

title: Weddings, Cafés, and Shared Social Life
summary: The research notes recall a time when Jewish and Muslim Tunisians attended one another's celebrations and spent time in the same restaurants and cafés. These were not merely places where people happened to be near one another. They created repeated…
content:
Themes: community · continuity · religious life · family · coexistence

The research notes recall a time when Jewish and Muslim Tunisians attended one another's celebrations and spent time in the same restaurants and cafés. These were not merely places where people happened to be near one another. They created repeated opportunities to talk, exchange news, and develop relationships beyond commercial transactions.

Albert Chiche's recollections, as recorded in the research discussion, point to a social world in which shared spaces helped make coexistence part of ordinary life. Jewish people attended Muslim weddings, and Muslim neighbours participated in Jewish celebrations. People met in familiar establishments and built relationships through repeated contact.

The notes also recognize that these larger gatherings have become less common as the Jewish population has declined. That change should not automatically be read as proof that personal relationships have disappeared. The reduction in gatherings may partly reflect the departure of families who once made them possible. The material therefore distinguishes between the decline of a community's social infrastructure and the complete breakdown of relations between individuals.

Source note: Based on interview-analysis notes concerning Daniel Cohen, Massimo, Albert Chiche, Samuel, and Participant A. This is a narrative synthesis, not a verbatim participant transcript.

relatedNarratives.title: Weddings Across Religious Lines
relatedNarratives.content:
Source: Daniel

Daniel remembers weddings as occasions when religious boundaries did not prevent people from sharing important moments. It was normal, in his account, for a Jewish person to attend a Muslim wedding and for a Muslim person to attend a Jewish wedding. These occasions were not described as unusual acts of interfaith outreach. They were part of the social life people already shared.

A wedding brought together relatives, friends, neighbours, and acquaintances. It offered a reason to meet, celebrate, eat, talk, and spend time with people beyond one's immediate household. Daniel's recollection suggests that the invitation itself was not necessarily understood through a religious lens. People attended because they knew the family, had a relationship with the hosts, or belonged to the same circle of neighbours and friends.

He places these celebrations alongside cafés, restaurants, and commercial relationships as examples of the ways people maintained contact. The common thread is familiarity. Relationships were sustained not only through declarations of mutual respect, but through participation in one another's lives.

This does not mean that every person had identical experiences or that religious differences disappeared. Rather, Daniel describes a social environment in which those differences did not automatically prevent people from sharing celebrations.

His account makes the wedding more than a private family event. It becomes a window into the wider network of relationships that connected people across religious communities in Tunisia.

relatedNarratives.title: The Café That No Longer Holds the Same Community
relatedNarratives.content:
Source: Albert

Albert remembers cafés as places where members of the Jewish community could meet, talk, and spend time together. In the past, he says, it was possible to enter a café and find several Jewish people gathered there. They would sit together, exchange news, and maintain the familiarity that came from seeing one another regularly.

Today, he describes a different scene. A person can enter a café and find no Jewish customers at all. The change is not simply that fewer people are present at a particular table. It reflects the shrinking of the community and the disappearance of some of the routines that once brought its members together.

The café mattered because it was an informal meeting place. It did not require a religious ceremony, a family celebration, or an organized event. People could meet as part of their ordinary day. These encounters helped sustain a sense of belonging beyond the home and synagogue.

Albert's recollection shows how demographic change can be felt in familiar public spaces. A café may continue operating, but the social world that once animated it can disappear. The building remains; the pattern of gathering changes.

His memory gives an intimate scale to the history of communal decline. Rather than describing the change only through population figures, he points to a simple experience: walking into a familiar café and no longer finding the people who once made it a place of shared community life.

title: Family Memory as a Way of Passing on Identity
summary: The interviews describe family as one of the ways Jewish Tunisian traditions continue from one generation to the next. The research notes explain that children learn not only through formal instruction but also by watching parents and grandparents: how they…
content:
Themes: community · continuity · religious life · family · coexistence

The interviews describe family as one of the ways Jewish Tunisian traditions continue from one generation to the next. The research notes explain that children learn not only through formal instruction but also by watching parents and grandparents: how they behave, how they treat neighbours, how they observe religious occasions, and how they participate in family and community life.

Massimo places particular importance on family and religious institutions. The notes emphasize the role of grandparents in teaching younger generations about religious customs, holidays, and family history. This form of transmission is often informal. A child may learn a practice by seeing it repeated over many years, rather than by receiving a formal lesson.

At the same time, the material raises a question about whether inherited practices will remain meaningful to younger people. Hearing about a tradition is not necessarily the same as feeling connected to it. Continuity depends not only on the presence of older generations, but also on whether younger people come to value what they have inherited.

Source note: Based on interview-analysis notes concerning Daniel Cohen, Massimo, Albert Chiche, Samuel, and Participant A. This is a narrative synthesis, not a verbatim participant transcript.

title: Why Albert Believes Education Matters
summary: Albert Chiche's perspective, as summarized in the research notes, places particular importance on education. He distinguishes between children hearing about their heritage at home and receiving more structured opportunities to learn about their history,…
content:
Themes: community · continuity · religious life · family · coexistence

Albert Chiche's perspective, as summarized in the research notes, places particular importance on education. He distinguishes between children hearing about their heritage at home and receiving more structured opportunities to learn about their history, religion, and cultural background.

The notes compare the educational experience described in Djerba with that in Tunis. Albert explains that Hebrew is part of the usual educational experience in Djerba, while Jewish children in Tunis do not necessarily receive the same kind of instruction. He also associates the strength of traditions in Djerba with the importance placed on teaching children from an early age.

This argument does not mean education alone can prevent emigration. The research discussion explicitly recognizes that people may remain deeply connected to their heritage and still leave for reasons connected to education, employment, family circumstances, or political uncertainty. Albert's point is instead about the conditions that help young people understand and value their identity. Formal learning may reinforce what families already teach, giving cultural transmission a more deliberate structure.

Source note: Based on interview-analysis notes concerning Daniel Cohen, Massimo, Albert Chiche, Samuel, and Participant A. This is a narrative synthesis, not a verbatim participant transcript.

title: The Difference Between Preserving Identity and Keeping People
summary: One of the central distinctions in the research material is that cultural continuity and demographic continuity are not the same thing. A community may preserve its traditions, teach its language, maintain religious institutions, and sustain a strong sense of…
content:
Themes: community · continuity · religious life · family · coexistence

One of the central distinctions in the research material is that cultural continuity and demographic continuity are not the same thing. A community may preserve its traditions, teach its language, maintain religious institutions, and sustain a strong sense of identity even as its population becomes smaller.

The comparison between Djerba and Tunis illustrates this tension. The notes describe stronger formal Jewish education in Djerba, including Hebrew instruction, but they also acknowledge that education and religious commitment do not guarantee that people will remain in Tunisia. Individuals may leave for opportunities elsewhere while retaining family ties, religious practices, and connections to their place of origin.

The same distinction appears in the discussion of La Goulette. The community's shrinking numbers have changed the scale of its institutions and gatherings, but the material does not treat that decline as automatic proof that identity has disappeared. Instead, it asks how much continuity can be sustained through family, religion, education, and relationships when fewer people remain physically present.

Source note: Based on interview-analysis notes concerning Daniel Cohen, Massimo, Albert Chiche, Samuel, and Participant A. This is a narrative synthesis, not a verbatim participant transcript.

relatedNarratives.title: From a Hundred Thousand to a Small Remnant
relatedNarratives.content:
Source: Albert

Albert places the decline of Tunisia's Jewish population within a sequence of departures that unfolded over several periods. He recalls that Tunisia once had around one hundred thousand Jews, while the community today is only a small fraction of that number. He identifies independence and the events surrounding the Bizerte conflict as important periods, and he also describes a significant departure in 1967.

According to his account, attacks on Jewish homes and businesses during the events of 1967 frightened many families. Some left for France, while others went to Israel. He describes the departures as occurring in stages rather than as one single movement. Different families left at different moments and for different reasons.

The consequences were not only numerical. When families left, the places where they had lived, worked, prayed, and gathered changed as well. A smaller population meant fewer businesses, fewer social gatherings, and greater difficulty maintaining the communal routines that had once been familiar.

Albert names several places where Jewish communities had existed, including Tunis, Sfax, Kef, Djerba, Bizerte, Nabeul, and Sousse. He also distinguishes between regions: some communities lived in identifiable Jewish quarters, while in other towns people lived alongside their neighbours within the same urban environment.

His account presents demographic decline as a transformation of an entire social landscape. The departure of families affected not only the number of people remaining, but also the everyday structures through which a community had once experienced its life.

relatedNarratives.title: A Community That Remains Active Despite Its Size
relatedNarratives.content:
Source: Daniel

Daniel describes the Jewish community in Tunis as much smaller than it once was, yet still connected through relationships that have survived over time. He says that people continue to know one another and maintain networks of familiarity. Those connections include residents who remain in Tunisia as well as people who grew up alongside Jewish families in earlier decades.

His account distinguishes population size from the strength of social relationships. A community can become numerically small without every connection disappearing. People may still recognize one another, work together, and maintain relationships built over many years.

Daniel also argues that the future depends on cooperation. He believes people should continue extending a hand to one another, acting responsibly within society, and passing these values on to their children. His emphasis is not only on preserving Jewish customs, but also on sustaining the relationships that have connected Jewish Tunisians with their neighbours.

The challenge, as he sees it, is generational. Older residents may remember a period when social contact was more frequent and the community was larger. Younger people may encounter a different environment, shaped by media and political narratives. Passing on the memory of everyday cooperation becomes one way to keep those relationships intelligible to the next generation.

Daniel's account presents continuity as an active responsibility. It requires people to keep cooperating, to remain present in society, and to teach younger generations that shared life is maintained through everyday conduct.

relatedNarratives.title: The Difference Between a Community's Number and Its Life
relatedNarratives.content:
Source: Albert

Albert gives several estimates of the Jewish population in Tunisia during the interview, including a figure of approximately three hundred people remaining across the country. He also recalls a much larger population in the past, around one hundred thousand. The figures in the transcript are estimates rather than a single verified count, but the contrast he is trying to describe is unmistakable: the community has undergone a profound demographic decline.

Yet Albert's account does not reduce community life to population statistics. He describes schools, synagogues, committees, businesses, family traditions, and relationships with neighbours. Some institutions remain active, while others have become harder to sustain. The synagogue still brings people together for prayer and conversation; committees help families in need; religious education continues in some settings.

He also remembers what has disappeared. Weddings that once brought families together are now less common because fewer Jewish families remain. Cafés that once held groups of Jewish friends may no longer contain a single Jewish customer. Commercial establishments and neighbourhood routines have changed alongside the population.

These details reveal why numbers alone cannot describe the experience of demographic decline. A smaller population affects the practical organization of religious services and institutions, but it also changes the social texture of everyday life.

Albert's testimony holds both realities together: a community can continue to preserve traditions and maintain institutions, while also experiencing losses that are difficult to reverse. Its remaining life deserves attention, but so does the scale of what has changed.

title: Living as Tunisian Beyond Religious Labels
summary: The research notes identify shared Tunisian identity as an important factor in Jewish-Muslim relations. Interview material describes people who understood one another first through shared experiences as neighbours, friends, and members of the same society,…
content:
Themes: community · continuity · religious life · family · coexistence

The research notes identify shared Tunisian identity as an important factor in Jewish-Muslim relations. Interview material describes people who understood one another first through shared experiences as neighbours, friends, and members of the same society, rather than allowing religious difference to determine every relationship.

Daniel Cohen's perspective, as summarized in the paper, emphasizes cooperation, mutual support, and responsibility within society. The notes also describe commercial and social interactions that brought Jewish and Muslim Tunisians into contact through shops, restaurants, cafés, and neighbourhood life.

The material does not suggest that differences or tensions never existed. It recognizes that political events and public narratives can influence how Jewish identity is perceived. One participant distinguishes between political disagreement and personal treatment, explaining that political views do not automatically determine how neighbours behave toward one another. The story therefore concerns the effort to maintain ordinary human relationships in a society where religious identity can sometimes be interpreted through events beyond the neighbourhood.

Source note: Based on interview-analysis notes concerning Daniel Cohen, Massimo, Albert Chiche, Samuel, and Participant A. This is a narrative synthesis, not a verbatim participant transcript.

Part V — A Russian-Jewish Family's Immigration to the United States

relatedNarratives.title: Human Relationships Before Religious Labels
relatedNarratives.content:
Source: Daniel

One of Daniel's strongest reflections concerns the way people understood one another in everyday life. He remembers relationships shaped by neighbourhood, work, friendship, and commerce. People knew one another through repeated encounters and shared routines. In that setting, religious identity was not necessarily the first thing that defined a relationship.

Daniel says that some people did not even like referring to someone as Jewish, because they felt that the label could create a separation where ordinary life had not necessarily contained one. He recalls people who had lived alongside one another for generations and who understood themselves first as members of the same Tunisian society.

His point is not that religious identities did not exist. Jewish and Muslim communities maintained their own religious practices, and each person could remain attached to a distinct tradition. Rather, he objects to treating those identities as if they automatically placed people in separate social worlds.

He repeatedly returns to the word “Tunisian.” For him, national belonging was a shared foundation. People could follow different religions while living in the same country, participating in the same society, and maintaining relationships that were not reducible to religious categories.

This perspective is particularly meaningful in a conversation about identity. Daniel's account shows how people may experience several dimensions of belonging at once. Religion can remain important without cancelling national identity or everyday human connection. His recollection asks the listener to consider how much is lost when a label is allowed to replace the complexity of a person's actual relationships.

relatedNarratives.title: Living Together in the Same Hara
relatedNarratives.content:
Source: Albert

When asked whether Jewish and Muslim residents could live in the same neighbourhood, Albert answers directly: in Djerba, they could live in the same Hara. He emphasizes that there was no inherent reason for this arrangement to create problems. People lived alongside one another, and neighbours helped each other when a need arose.

His answer challenges the assumption that a Jewish quarter necessarily meant a completely closed or socially isolated space. Albert describes the Hara as a place where people of different religions could share the same local environment. Their lives intersected through proximity, work, and everyday assistance.

He also describes cooperation as a normal feature of daily life. People worked alongside one another, respected one another, and developed genuine affection. His recollection does not suggest that everyone had to share the same beliefs. Instead, it suggests that people could maintain their religious identities while participating in a common neighbourhood.

The example of Shabbat assistance gives this account a practical dimension, but the larger point is about the social meaning of living together. A neighbour was someone nearby, someone whose needs could be understood, and someone who might offer help in return.

Albert's testimony is valuable because it describes coexistence through lived arrangements rather than slogans. The shared Hara was not simply a symbol. It was a place where people encountered one another as neighbours and built relationships through the ordinary responsibilities of daily life.

relatedNarratives.title: A Tunisian Identity That Includes Jewish Life
relatedNarratives.content:
Source: Albert

When asked about the relationship between Jewish identity and Tunisia, Albert speaks firmly about national belonging. He says that the Jewish people he is describing are Tunisian: Tunisia is their country, and the Tunisian flag is their flag. He explains that they live according to their religion while remaining part of Tunisian society and respecting the country's laws.

This distinction matters in a conversation where Jewish identity can be treated as if it automatically indicates a political position. Albert rejects that assumption. He separates being Jewish from being a Zionist and emphasizes that his sense of belonging is rooted in Tunisia.

His words also connect with his recollections of everyday life. He describes people working together, helping neighbours, sharing neighbourhoods, and maintaining relationships across religious lines. National identity, in this account, is not only a statement about citizenship. It is reflected in the ordinary experience of living alongside other Tunisians.

Albert acknowledges that political events, particularly the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, can affect conversations and create tension. Yet he distinguishes those discussions from the relationships people maintain with their neighbours. Political disagreement does not necessarily erase years of familiarity.

His testimony is important because it allows a participant to define his own identity in his own terms. Rather than treating religion and nationality as competing categories, Albert describes them as parts of a life that can coexist.

title: Leaving the Soviet Union Was a Risk, Not a Simple Decision
summary: The interview notes describe the decision to leave the Soviet Union as a choice shaped by both hope and serious risk. The family wanted greater freedom and opportunity, but leaving was not as simple as purchasing a ticket and moving abroad. They needed an…
content:
Themes: immigration · family · adaptation · work · belonging

The interview notes describe the decision to leave the Soviet Union as a choice shaped by both hope and serious risk. The family wanted greater freedom and opportunity, but leaving was not as simple as purchasing a ticket and moving abroad. They needed an invitation from a relative overseas, connected to the process through which Jewish families could reunite with relatives who had been separated by the upheavals of the Second World War.

Once the invitation was obtained, the family had to petition the Soviet government for permission to leave. The notes explain that this could involve giving up Soviet citizenship and becoming officially stateless while travelling as refugees. The danger was that a rejected application could expose the family's intention to emigrate. Since employment was controlled by the state, a person whose application was refused could find it extremely difficult to obtain another job.

The decision therefore involved uncertainty at every stage: whether permission would be granted, whether the family could leave safely, and whether they would be able to rebuild their lives elsewhere. The interview presents emigration not as a single moment of departure, but as a risk taken in the hope of a freer future.

Source note: Based on the user's interview notes and transcript fragments. Details should be checked against the original recording before publication.

title: Letters Written in Code
summary: Before the family left, communication with relatives abroad had to be handled carefully. The interview notes explain that mail from the United States or Israel could be read before it reached its recipient. A letter containing explicit details about plans to…
content:
Themes: immigration · family · adaptation · work · belonging

Before the family left, communication with relatives abroad had to be handled carefully. The interview notes explain that mail from the United States or Israel could be read before it reached its recipient. A letter containing explicit details about plans to emigrate could create problems for the people involved.

The family therefore developed a code before the relatives separated. Ordinary descriptions of the weather could carry meanings that would not be obvious to someone reading the letter. A sentence about sunshine or rain could communicate something more important without stating it directly.

The notes describe the code as something agreed upon in person, before the relative left. That detail matters because it shows how communication itself had to be planned around surveillance. The family could not simply explain what was happening in writing. They had to preserve a private language within ordinary correspondence.

This small practice reveals the atmosphere surrounding the decision to leave. Even a letter between family members could not be assumed to be private. Maintaining contact required caution, preparation, and trust.

Source note: Based on the user's interview notes and transcript fragments. Details should be checked against the original recording before publication.

title: The Long Journey Through Vienna and Rome
summary: The interview notes trace the family's route to the United States in 1976. They first flew to Vienna, where they stayed for approximately two weeks. They then lived in Rome for around three months while waiting for visa approval. In total, the journey from…
content:
Themes: immigration · family · adaptation · work · belonging

The interview notes trace the family's route to the United States in 1976. They first flew to Vienna, where they stayed for approximately two weeks. They then lived in Rome for around three months while waiting for visa approval. In total, the journey from leaving to arriving in the United States lasted about three and a half months.

This was not a direct move from one home to another. The family had to wait in different places while the paperwork and permission process continued. The notes make clear that the journey involved uncertainty and a period of living between countries, without yet knowing exactly when the next stage would begin.

The route also helps put the decision to emigrate into perspective. The family's hope for freedom and opportunity required patience and a willingness to live through an extended transition. Arrival in the United States was the end of one difficult process, but it was also the beginning of another: rebuilding a life in a country where familiar institutions, careers, and social networks would have to be established again.

Source note: Based on the user's interview notes and transcript fragments. Details should be checked against the original recording before publication.

title: A Child Learns English by Being Immersed
summary: The interviewee describes adapting to American life as relatively manageable because she was still a child. She arrived without speaking English and entered fourth grade. Within a few months, she had learned enough to navigate school and daily life. The notes…
content:
Themes: immigration · family · adaptation · work · belonging

The interviewee describes adapting to American life as relatively manageable because she was still a child. She arrived without speaking English and entered fourth grade. Within a few months, she had learned enough to navigate school and daily life. The notes compare the experience to being immersed completely in a language and learning through necessity.

Television also became part of that process. Watching programs and cartoons, including The Flintstones and The Brady Bunch, helped her become familiar with English. Her mother was an English teacher and already spoke the language well, but the interviewee recalls that learning happened primarily through immersion rather than formal lessons at home.

The interview also contrasts her experience with that of her older sister, who was seventeen and had just finished high school in Russia. Her sister felt attached to the friends and life she was leaving behind, and the transition was more emotionally difficult. The difference suggests that adapting to a new country depends not only on the opportunities available, but also on age, attachment, and whether a person is ready to leave the old environment.

title: A Doctor Has to Begin Again

content:
Themes: immigration · family · adaptation · work · belonging

The interview notes describe the father's professional transition after arriving in the United States. He had worked as a doctor for decades, but his previous qualifications did not allow him to resume his profession immediately. He had to study for the required examinations and improve his English before he could obtain a licence.

For approximately a year, he remained at home studying intensively. The notes describe a demanding schedule, with preparation taking up much of his day. He had to pass the relevant English test and medical examinations, and then complete a residency alongside people who were much younger. He was around forty-five, while some of the other residents were approximately twenty-five.

This experience illustrates the professional cost of starting over after migration. The family had moved in search of opportunity, but the father could not simply transfer his career from one country to another. Years of experience did not remove the need to prove his qualifications again. His path shows how migration can create opportunity while also requiring people to repeat stages of professional development they had already completed.
